Triggers.value: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I think about how life would have been different if the event had not occurred
go along with whatever others want to feel safe
Being reminded of the event by others

Threat.value: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard

Memory.value: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
When I remember the event I feel intense rage
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

Negative Appraisals.value: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it
I feel like an object, not like a person

vignette: Mei Lin was nine when her mother’s hands became the quiet architecture of her days. The discipline was physical and deliberate, anchored in the narrow hallways of their childhood home. Her mother would press her thumbs into the hollows of Mei Lin’s collarbones, pinning her wrists while the house hummed around them. What frightened Mei Lin most was the suddenness of it. A quick shift in her mother’s shoulders, a sharp step forward, and Mei Lin’s body would lock before her mind could catch up. She had come to believe that she was a weak person, something easily held and firmly moved. Years later, what happened to her felt deeply unfair, nothing having been done about it, not by her family, not by the relatives who noticed but turned their gaze away. She felt like an object, not a person, handled rather than seen, and that quiet sense of being managed settled into the marrow of her days. As Mei Lin grew, those early moments layered into steady patterns. She went along with whatever others wanted, nodding through conversations and yielding her space, because compliance kept the quiet safety intact. When her aunt mentioned the old stories of her childhood, or when a coworker brought up the steady, watchful nature of her mother, Mei Lin quietly stepped back, sidestepping the reminders that others offered so freely. She found it hard to reach deliberately into the past; the memories stayed just out of grasp, tucked behind the everyday. Sometimes, the feeling of the event would strike without any picture at all, a sudden wave of heat and tightness in her stomach that left her standing still in the middle of a room. When the memories did surface, they carried a sharp rage that surprised her, leaving her breathless until it passed. She often wondered how life would have been different if she had simply slipped through that house unnoticed, if she had been left alone to grow without the weight of those familiar hands. Now twenty-four, working as an urban planner, Mei Lin’s days map themselves between desk and site. Her corner office is a familiar rhythm, but the real test comes during planning committees and neighborhood walk-throughs. She only feels safe within a very limited number of places: her apartment, the exact chair in the studio, the wall panel where she can brace her back. When a colleague rises too quickly, or when someone gestures across the table, Mei Lin’s guard goes up immediately. Her stomach turns, a steady nausea blooming whenever she is being examined, even in the most routine moments. It is why she dreads the physical checkups that align with her work trips; the doctor’s hands on her shoulders send that familiar heat down her arms, and she becomes painfully aware of being seen, her posture remembering its place beneath the weight of scrutiny. In the planning studio, where junior planners constantly shift blueprints and stride past her desk, Mei Lin finds her attention fraying alongside her rising pulse. The sudden movements and her difficulty concentrating arrive together, a quiet storm of physical awareness. They co-exist in her days without tugging one another forward. At home, the quiet of her kitchen holds her, but the edges of her world feel increasingly tight. She has not broken, but she has been narrowing her life to fit her safe zone, trading spontaneous gatherings for predictable routines, and postponing appointments that require her to be touched or watched. What finally brought her to seek help was a site visit to a historic district, where a contractor’s quick hand resting on her shoulder left her nauseous and silent, staring at the ground while the rest of the team discussed sightlines. She went to the clinic hoping to untangle the knot, to understand why her body still braces for the hold, and what she fears most is that she will spend the rest of her life waiting to be moved. She hopes, though, that the memories will settle into something she can hold, rather than something that holds her.
